marble.name: Adding two two-digit numbers
marble.subject: Mathematics
marble.description: Add and subtract two two-digit numbers using concrete objects, pictorial representations, and mental methods
marble.prompt: Can you add or subtract two two-digit numbers — like '43 + 28' — using counters, a drawing, or working it out in their head?

cluster.summary: Your child is building a strong foundation in addition and subtraction, learning to combine and separate numbers up to 20 using objects, drawings, and mental strategies.

misconceptions: Failing to compose the ten: adding tens (50) and ones (11) and writing them side by side (511) or keeping 51
Smaller-from-larger subtraction: 63−28 done as 8−3 in the ones, answer 45
Counting every unit and losing the ten-structure (not treating a ten-rod as one ten)
Misaligning tens and ones when recording without a place-value mat
representations: Base-ten blocks with a place-value mat (compose/decompose a ten)
Number line (jumps for adding; count-up for difference)
authoredAnswer: 61 and 35. For 34+27: 30+20=50 and 4+7=11, exchange ten ones for a ten → 61. For 63−28: too few ones, exchange a ten for ten ones (63 as 50+13), 13−8=5 and 50−20=30 → 35.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: The child records 50 and 11 but never exchanges the eleven ones for a ten; writes 511 or 51
wrongAnswers.fix: Have the child physically swap ten of the eleven ones for one ten-rod on the mat, then read the result. Name it: ten ones is the same as one ten.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: The ones column of 63−28 is done as 8−3 with no decomposition; answer 45
wrongAnswers.fix: On the mat, show 63 cannot give 8 ones from only 3, so a ten must be broken open first (63 = 50+13). Check by adding 45+28.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: The child breaks rods apart to count all in ones, or recounts the whole set, rather than operating with rods as tens
wrongAnswers.fix: Do NOT stop them handling the blocks or drill exchange in isolation — treating a rod as one 'ten' is a maturing shift. Keep pairing the two readings aloud ('that's ten ones AND one ten') each time they exchange, so unitising develops.
